note: Every number here was checked against the linked source on the date above. Numbers computed by Terra Vox from NASA/NOAA files live in data/reference.json and data/features, and are shown with their method.

wildfires.lead: MODIS on NASA's Terra satellite flags every 1 km pixel where a fire burns hot enough to stand out from its surroundings, day and night, and has done so since 2000.
wildfires.measures: Active fire detections: where a fire was burning when the satellite passed, not how much land burned.

facts.text: More of the most extreme wildfire events (top 0.01% by fire radiative power) in 2023 than in 2003. The last seven years include the six most extreme.
facts.source: Cunningham, Williamson & Bowman 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution, from MODIS

facts.text: Global burned area fell by about a quarter from 1998 to 2015, mostly as savannas and grasslands were converted to farmland. Fewer fires overall, but fiercer ones in forests.
Pixel size of VIIRS, the instrument behind NASA's EIC fire visualization on side B. About three times more detailed than MODIS, so it catches smaller, cooler fires.

instruments.name: MODIS on Terra
instruments.role: Side A frames: 1 km active-fire detections, 2001–2025

instruments.name: VIIRS on Suomi NPP / NOAA-20 / NOAA-21
instruments.role: Side B: NASA EIC fire radiative power visualization, 2024–present

caveats: Each frame is one 8-day window in mid-August: the northern fire season. Africa's and Australia's peak seasons fall outside it.
Counting fire pixels says where fires burned, not how intense they were or how much land they burned, so a year can have fewer detections and worse fires.

Terra left its formation in October 2022 and has been drifting to an earlier overpass time; by mid-2026 it crossed the equator about two hours closer to dawn. Fires peak in the afternoon, so recent Terra years likely under-count.
NASA plans to begin shutting down Terra and Aqua in late 2026 or early 2027; VIIRS carries the fire record forward.

sources.name: NASA FIRMS: Fire Information for Resource Management System

sea_level.lead: Since 1992 a relay of radar altimeter satellites has measured the height of the ocean surface to within a few centimetres, revisiting every track about every ten days.
sea_level.measures: Sea surface height anomaly: how far the sea surface sits above or below its 1993–2012 average at each place.

facts.text: Average global sea level has risen about 4 inches since 1993, and the yearly rate of rise has more than doubled.
The rate of rise grew from 2.1 mm a year in 1993 to 4.5 mm a year by the end of 2023.
facts.source: Hamlington et al. 2024, Communications Earth & Environment

facts.text: Rise in 2025, well below the expected 0.44 cm a year: La Niña rain parked extra water on land in the Amazon basin. 2024 had risen 0.59 cm. NASA expects the rise to resume as that water drains back.

instruments.name: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich
instruments.role: Current reference satellite; Sentinel-6B followed in November 2025

caveats: NASA's gridded sea-surface-height layer in GIBS (JPL MEaSUREs) ends in January 2019, so these frames stop at 2018. The official record on the chart continues to 2025.
Each frame is one 5-day snapshot near October 1. El Niño years (1997, 2015) bulge the Pacific, so single frames wobble around the long-term rise.
Map colours show regional height differences. The global mean is a small shift of the whole picture, which is why the sound changes slowly.
The reference line has no glacial isostatic adjustment, so its trend reads about 0.3 mm a year lower than NASA's corrected figure.

sources.name: NASA Sea Level Change portal: global mean sea level
NASA SVS: Global Mean Sea Level 1993–2025

air_quality.lead: Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) comes mostly from burning fuel in vehicles, power plants and industry. The Dutch–Finnish OMI instrument on NASA's Aura satellite has mapped it every day since October 2004.
air_quality.measures: Tropospheric NO₂ column: the number of NO₂ molecules above each square centimetre of ground, in the lowest ~10 km of air.

facts.text: Share of the world's population living where WHO air-quality guideline levels were not met in 2019. Outdoor air pollution caused an estimated 4.2 million premature deaths that year.
facts.source: World Health Organization fact sheet, October 24, 2024

facts.text: NO₂ fell by this much across the United States from 2005 to 2014 as power plants and cars got cleaner, while parts of China rose by a similar amount and India kept climbing.
facts.source: Duncan et al. 2016, Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres (NASA)

facts.text: TEMPO, launched in April 2023, measures NO₂ over North America every daylight hour from geostationary orbit. Side B plays its rush-hour cycle from NASA's EIC.

instruments.name: OMI on Aura
instruments.role: Side A frames: daily global NO₂, 13 × 24 km pixels

instruments.name: TEMPO
instruments.role: Side B: hourly NO₂ over North America (NASA EIC)

caveats: Each frame is a 3-day March mosaic, so wind and weather drive most frame-to-frame change: that noise is this theme's sound.
The global average barely moves because big regional changes cancel out: cleaner air over the US and Europe, dirtier air over South Asia.
OMI's 'row anomaly' (since 2007) blanks part of every swath. Gaps are skipped, not counted as clean air.
A column measured from space is not the concentration at street level, and the top of the GIBS palette saturates over the dirtiest cities.

sources.name: NASA Earth Observatory: NO₂ getting better, getting worse

greenhouse_gases.lead: Methane (CH₄) is the second-largest driver of human-caused warming after carbon dioxide. AIRS on NASA's Aqua satellite measures it in the mid-troposphere, about 7 km up.
greenhouse_gases.measures: Methane volume mixing ratio at the 400 hPa pressure level: methane molecules per billion molecules of air.

facts.text: Methane in 2024 stood 166% above its pre-industrial level (before 1750), at 1,942 ppb. Carbon dioxide was 52% above and nitrous oxide 25%.
facts.source: WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin No. 21, October 2025

facts.text: Over 20 years, a tonne of fossil methane traps about 80 times as much heat as a tonne of CO₂ (GWP-20 of 82.5; about 30 over 100 years).
facts.source: IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Table 7.15

facts.text: Methane breaks down in about a decade, far faster than CO₂, so cutting it is the quickest way to slow near-term warming.

instruments.name: AIRS on Aqua
instruments.role: Side A frames: monthly methane at 400 hPa, 2,378 infrared channels

instruments.name: NASA GEOS model
instruments.role: Side B: NASA EIC volumetric methane for 2021 (a model, informed by observations)

caveats: AIRS sees methane about 7 km up, where it is lower and smoother than at the surface, so these values sit below NOAA's surface line. The trends agree.
Each frame is the August monthly mean, which removes the seasonal cycle; El Niño and wetland swings still move single years.
Aqua is drifting and NASA plans to begin shutting it down in late 2026 or early 2027.
GIBS stores methane in 2 ppb colour steps, so every value here is rounded to within about 1 ppb.
